questions.stem: Comment on “If Aristotle were Chinese, his logic would be different” using the Sapir–Whorf hypothesis.
questions.referenceAnswer:
This statement invites us to consider how language, culture and thought interact, which is precisely the concern of the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis. The hypothesis holds that the language we speak influences, and possibly determines, the way we perceive and conceptualize the world. It is interpreted in two versions. The determinism (strong) version claims that language determines our thinking, so that different languages may lead to unique ways of understanding the world; the relativism (weak) version holds that the similarity between languages is only relative: the greater their structural differentiation, the more diverse will be the conceptualization of the world, for culture affects the way we think through language, especially in our classification of the experienced world.

If Aristotle had been Chinese, the strong version would predict that he would have inherited a different conceptual apparatus encoded in Chinese and hence a different logic; Aristotle's logic would then be a product of the Greek language rather than of universal reason. The weak version offers a more defensible reading: Chinese categories, metaphors and culturally loaded expressions might have led a Chinese Aristotle to different habitual conceptualizations, for example more holistic and context-based styles of argument than the formal-analytic logic of Greek philosophy, yet it does not follow that he could not think in the Greek manner.

Most evidence supports only the weak version. Speakers of different languages can translate, borrow concepts and understand one another, which the strong version cannot explain. A balanced comment is therefore that language is a guide to, not a prison of, thought: if Aristotle were Chinese, his logic would very likely have been expressed differently and its habitual emphases might have differed, but the human logical capacity itself is not determined by the particular language one speaks. Language, culture and thought mutually influence one another rather than standing in one-way determination.
questions.analysis: 考Chapter 10 Sapir-Whorf假说（笔记Chapter10 p.21）。答题套路：先述假说及两个版本（决定论/强式：语言决定思维；相对论/弱式：语言影响习惯性思维，结构差异越大概念化差异越大），再用其评论该命题：亚里士多德的逻辑或受希腊语影响，若为汉人其习惯性概念化可能不同，但语言并不完全决定思维（跨语言可译、可相互理解反驳强式）。失分点：只背定义不结合评论；一边倒支持强式。

questions.stem: Revise VP → (Aux) V PP so it can generate “Her dog always sleeps under it” and “These pigs can sometimes stay in the house.”
questions.referenceAnswer: Add an optional adverb slot between Aux and V: VP -> (Aux) (Adv) V PP. Because the adverb is bracketed as optional, the revised rule still generates all the original (Aux) V PP strings, so nothing that the old rule generated is lost.

questions.stem: Distinguish register from regional and social dialects. Explain how a teacher's view of language can shape foreign-language teaching.
questions.referenceAnswer:
语域按使用情境区分（variety according to use）；地域/社会方言按使用者区分。语域可从 field、mode、tenor 描述。语言观会影响课程、材料和目标：形式取向突出结构，功能取向兼顾交际功能，交际取向重视交际能力。

展开（英文作答参考）：Register is a "variety according to use", while regional dialects and sociolects are "varieties according to user". One's dialect shows who you are and where you are from, while the register shows what you are doing and with whom. Register is analyzed on three dimensions: field (the purpose or subject matter - why and about what we communicate), mode (the means - how we communicate, e.g. face-to-face talk vs a letter) and tenor (the relationship between participants - with whom, e.g. close friends vs the boss). A speaker keeps one dialect but shifts registers constantly, e.g. salt at the dinner table vs sodium chloride in the laboratory.

As for the second question, as S. Pit Corder says, the way we teach language is influenced, even determined, by what we believe language to be. At the preparatory level, specialists' views of language guide syllabus design and material development; at the classroom level, a teacher's understanding of the nature of language influences what and how he teaches. A formal/structural view of language highlights sentence patterns and grammatical accuracy; a functional view (e.g. Halliday) specifies content not only in grammatical elements but also in the functional items students need to communicate successfully; a communicative view takes the development of learners' communicative competence - grammatical, sociolinguistic, discourse and strategic - as the objective, favoring meaningful, interactive activities. The teacher's view of language thus shapes the curriculum, the materials, the methodology and even the tests.

questions.stem: Explain: symbol, morality play, theme, negative capability, revenge tragedy, Imagism, slave narrative and Chicano literature.
questions.referenceAnswer: (1) Symbol: a person, object, image or action that signifies more than its literal meaning and conveys a further abstract idea or emotion; unlike a passing metaphor it is sustained through the work (e.g. the green light in The Great Gatsby, the scarlet A in The Scarlet Letter). (2) Morality play: a medieval dramatic genre in which abstract virtues, vices and forces are personified to dramatize the moral conflict for the human soul; the best-known example is Everyman. (3) Theme: the central or controlling idea a work explores; it is implied through plot, character and imagery rather than directly stated, and must be distinguished from the mere subject. (4) Negative capability: Keats's term for the poet's capacity to accept uncertainties, mysteries and doubts 'without any irritable reaching after fact and reason' — an ideal of open-mindedness, of 'letting the mind be a thoroughfare for all thoughts' (高分笔记2, p31). (5) Revenge tragedy: an Elizabethan-Jacobean dramatic genre in which the plot is driven by the hero's quest to avenge a murder or grave wrong, typically involving feigned madness, a play-within-the-play and the avenger's own death; Kyd initiated the type and Shakespeare's Hamlet is its supreme example. (6) Imagism: an early-20th-century poetic movement led by Ezra Pound, characterized by the use of precise imagery, clear and economical language and free rhythm; Pound's 'In a Station of the Metro' is the classic example (高分笔记5, p32-33). (7) Slave narrative: autobiographical accounts written by formerly enslaved people (e.g. Frederick Douglass) recounting the horrors of bondage, the quest for literacy and escape, and indicting the institution of slavery; a formative genre of African-American literature. (8) Chicano literature: the literature of Mexican-Americans, exploring bicultural and bilingual experience, ethnic identity, discrimination and the struggle for social justice in the United States.
questions.analysis: 八个术语横跨戏剧（morality play、revenge tragedy）、诗学（symbol、theme、negative capability、Imagism）与美国族裔文学（slave narrative、Chicano literature），须逐条编号作答，每个术语按'定义+特征+代表作家作品'三步写。关键归属：negative capability 必须归于济慈（笔记2 p31），Imagism 必须归于庞德（笔记5 p32）。常见失分点：把 morality play 与 miracle play 混淆、把 slave narrative 写成一般奴隶制历史叙述而漏掉'自传体'这一文体特征。

questions.stem: Define phonology, allophones, suprasegmental features and TG grammar. Distinguish morpheme/allomorph and theme/rheme.
questions.referenceAnswer: Phonology studies language-specific sound systems; allophones are context-dependent realizations of one phoneme; suprasegmentals include stress, intonation and tone; TG grammar models grammatical sentences using finite phrase-structure and transformational rules. A morpheme is a minimal meaningful unit; allomorphs are variants of one morpheme. Theme is the message's starting point; rheme is the remainder.
questions.analysis: 五个定义跨Ch3/4/5：音系学研究特定语言的声音系统与规律（笔记Chapter3 p.9）；音位变体 allophone 是音位在特定语境中的实现（pp.9-10，互补分布）；超音段特征包括重音、语调、声调（p.13）；TG语法用有限规则生成且只生成合语法句、含深层/表层结构与转换规则（Chapter5 pp.12-13）；词素为最小有意义的单位、词素变体为同一词素的变体（Chapter4 pp.2-3）；主位为信息起点、述位为其余部分（Chapter5 p.20）。失分点：allomorph 与 allophone、morpheme 的对应关系张冠李戴；漏 theme 未必等于语法主语。

questions.stem: Using the data car [kʰaː], scar [sk=aː], “this car” [ðɪs kʰaː], discard [dɪsk=aːd], explain raised h and = and state the aspiration rule.
questions.referenceAnswer: In these narrow transcriptions the raised h (as in [k_h]) is the diacritic marking aspiration, and the raised equals sign (as in [k=]) marks an unaspirated sound. The data show that /k/ is aspirated ([k_h]) word-initially in car and in "this car" where k begins a stressed syllable, but unaspirated ([k=]) in the /s/-clusters of scar and discard. The aspiration rule therefore states: voiceless stops (/p, t, k/) are aspirated when they occur initially in a stressed syllable (pin, team, cool, car), but they are unaspirated when they follow /s/ in the same syllable (spin, scar, discard). Aspiration is thus a non-distinctive, predictable feature in English, and [k_h] and [k=] are allophones of the single phoneme /k/ in complementary distribution.

questions.stem: (1) Compare “Mike broke the teapot” with “The teapot was broken by Mike” in information structure. (2) Name/explain grammatical cohesion with examples. (3) For “A: Have you seen Peter today? B: Well, if I didn't deny seeing him I wouldn't be telling a lie,” identify the flouted maxim and infer B's meaning.
questions.referenceAnswer:
(1) The two clauses describe the same event, but their information structure differs. The constituent that stands for the starting point of the message is the theme; all the rest is the rheme. In "Mike broke the teapot" the theme is Mike, the person known to both speaker and hearer, and the clause answers "What did Mike do?"; in "The teapot was broken by Mike" the theme is the teapot, and the clause answers "What happened to the teapot?".
(2) Grammatical cohesion is achieved in three ways. Reference: items refer to something else for their interpretation, looking backward (anaphoric) or forward (cataphoric); personal reference by pronouns ("John is my brother. He came here yesterday."), demonstrative reference (this/that) and comparative reference (as...as). Substitution: one linguistic item replaces another - nominal substitutes (one, ones, some, same), verbal substitutes (do, does) and clausal substitutes (so, not). Ellipsis, "something left unsaid": nominal ("Would you like to hear another verse? I know three more."), verbal ("John brought some apples and Amy some pears.") and clausal ellipsis ("How many hours did you do lessons? Ten hours.").
(3) B's reply is deliberately obscure and roundabout instead of the simple "Yes, I have". This flouts the maxim of manner (avoid obscurity of expression). Assuming cooperation, A infers a conversational implicature: if B answers in such a twisted way, it must be because the direct answer would cost face or invite trouble; the implication is that B has in fact seen Peter today.

questions.stem: (1) In the transcriptions, pear and “this pear” show [pʰ], while spare and despair show [p⁼]; explain these diacritics and infer the aspiration rule. (2) Compare “a redcoat”/“a red coat” and “a bluebird”/“a blue bird.” (3) Describe particle movement using “John turned off the machine” and “John turned the machine off”; say whether event meaning changes. (4) Explain: Diner: “Waiter, what's this fly doing in my soup?” Waiter: “Madam, I believe that's the backstroke.”
questions.referenceAnswer:
(1) The raised h is the diacritic for aspiration: [p_h] in pear and "this pear" is aspirated, while [p=] in spare and despair is unaspirated. The aspiration rule: voiceless stops are aspirated when they occur initially in a stressed syllable, but unaspirated after /s/ in the same syllable (spin, spare, despair); [p_h] and [p=] are allophones of /p/ in complementary distribution.
(2) In "a redcoat" and "a bluebird" an indefinite article is followed by a compound noun: primary stress falls on the first element and the meaning is lexicalized (a redcoat = a British soldier; a bluebird = a kind of bird). In "a red coat" and "a blue bird" the article is followed by a modifier plus a noun: stress falls on the noun and the meaning is literal (a coat that is red; a bird that is blue). Compounds show that the meaning of a compound is not always the sum of its parts.
(3) "Turn" and "off" form one discontinuous constituent of the verb phrase, and "off" is a verbal particle. By the particle movement transformation, when a verbal particle is followed by a noun phrase, the particle can be reordered to the right of the noun phrase: John turned off the machine -> John turned the machine off. The operation involves reordering only; the core event meaning is unchanged (with a pronoun object only John turned it off is possible).
(4) The diner's question is not really a request for information but an indirect complaint, meaning roughly "Why is there a fly in my soup?". The waiter deliberately takes the literal reading and answers it as if the fly were really performing an action ("doing the backstroke"), giving an irrelevant/literal response instead of an apology. This flouts the maxim of quantity (and relevance), and the flout generates the implicature that produces the joke.

questions.stem: Define the Critical Period Hypothesis and comment on evidence/limitations concerning age and second-language learning.
questions.referenceAnswer:
The Critical Period Hypothesis (CPH) claims that there is a period, with the optimal age within roughly the first ten years of life, when language acquisition takes place naturally and effectively. In second language research it rests on two assumptions: (1) the neurological basis of language in children is different from that in adults; (2) children outperform adults in all aspects of second language acquisition.

Evidence and limitations. The truth value of the first assumption remains an open issue, because the exact neurological difference and its consequences for learning are hard to verify. The second assumption has been challenged by later studies: adults often learn certain aspects of language (morphology, syntax, vocabulary) faster at the initial stage, and late learners can still reach very high proficiency. What later research does support is a child advantage in pronunciation: early starters are far more likely to acquire native-like accent. At the same time adults are advantageous in cognitive capabilities, such as analytic ability, metalinguistic awareness and learning strategies. Moreover, age does not change the route of acquisition: children and adults pass through broadly similar developmental stages, differing mainly in rate and ultimate attainment.

Comment. In its strong form ("children are better at everything") the hypothesis is untenable for L2 learning; a weak interpretation is defensible - there may be sensitive periods for particular aspects of language, notably phonology, and each age has its own advantages. For teaching, this means age alone does not decide success: instruction should exploit adults' cognitive strengths while providing rich early exposure to pronunciation, and motivation, aptitude and learning strategies remain decisive at any age.

questions.stem: Describe the non-standard English constructions in “We can't got none” and “He just lazy.”
questions.referenceAnswer: In "We can't got none" two non-standard features appear. First, multiple negation: negation is marked both by "can't" and by "none" ("We can't get any"), where Standard English allows only one negative marker in the clause. Second, non-standard verb morphology: "got" is used after the modal instead of the bare form "get". The whole sentence corresponds to Standard English "We can't get any". In "He just lazy" the copula is deleted: Standard English requires "He is just lazy". This zero copula is a systematic feature of several non-standard varieties, especially where the missing form would be a contracted 's. Both sentences show that non-standard varieties are rule-governed rather than merely "wrong": their grammar differs from the standard variety in regular, describable ways.

questions.stem: Explain the Beat Generation, Jazz Age, interior monologue, confessional poetry and international theme.
questions.referenceAnswer: (1) Beat Generation: a group of post-WWII American writers (Jack Kerouac, Allen Ginsberg) who rejected mainstream middle-class conformity and materialism, celebrating road travel, jazz, drifters and spiritual quest; Ginsberg's Howl is widely regarded as the central poem of the Beat movement and Kerouac's On the Road its classic novel, in which 'the road itself is the goal' (高分笔记6, p1, p3-5). (2) Jazz Age: the name for the America of the 1920s, an era of jazz music, post-war prosperity, consumerism and loosened morals; Fitzgerald was famous for his depiction of the Jazz Age, and The Great Gatsby is its classic text (高分笔记5, p13). (3) Interior monologue: a stream-of-consciousness narrative technique that presents the flow of a character's inner thoughts, impressions, feelings and free associations directly, without conventional dialogue or authorial intervention; practiced by Joyce, Woolf and Faulkner (高分笔记3, p15; 高分笔记5, p25). (4) Confessional poetry: a mid-20th-century American school of poetry (Robert Lowell, Sylvia Plath, Anne Sexton) that makes the poet's private life — guilt, mental illness, family trauma, marriage — the explicit subject of intense first-person verse. (5) International theme: the term for Henry James's characteristic subject: the encounter and contrast between American innocence, energy and idealism and European sophistication, tradition and corruption, dramatized through characters who cross national and cultural boundaries.

questions.stem: Answer five literature prompts: summarize The Great Gatsby; describe Faulkner's characteristic techniques; analyze Willy Loman through the American Dream; explain Poe's unity of effect; discuss Transcendentalism's definition, features and writers.
questions.referenceAnswer: (1) The Great Gatsby: Narrator Nick Carraway tells of Jay Gatsby, a mysterious millionaire who reinvented himself from poor James Gatz to win back Daisy Buchanan, whom he loved five years earlier. Through lavish parties he reconnects with Daisy, but she cannot renounce the security of her class represented by Tom. Driving Gatsby's car, Daisy kills Tom's mistress Myrtle; Gatsby takes the blame and is shot by Myrtle's husband Wilson, while Tom and Daisy retreat into their money and almost no one attends Gatsby's funeral. The novel exposes the corruption and emptiness of the American Dream — 'So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past' (高分笔记5, p10, p14). (2) Faulkner's characteristic techniques: stream of consciousness, which allows readers to enter the characters' minds and feel themselves participants rather than observers (Benjy's section of The Sound and the Fury); multiple point of view, letting different narrators react differently to the same events so that truth is difficult to reach; mythic construction of Yoknapatawpha County (Jefferson modeled on Oxford, Mississippi) as a microcosm of the South; themes of the decline of the Southern aristocracy after the Civil War (高分笔记5, p22-25). (3) Willy Loman: an aging traveling salesman who has built his life on the American Dream of easy success and of being 'well liked'; unable to accept his ordinary life and his failure, he commits suicide so that his family can collect the insurance money. Miller described the play as 'the tragedy of a man who gave his life, or sold it, in pursuit of the American Dream': the dream turns a human being into a product and destroys both Willy and his sons (高分笔记6, p25, p27). (4) Poe's unity of effect: Poe's theory (set out in 'The Philosophy of Composition') that a short tale or poem should be planned so that every element — plot, character, setting, tone, and a length readable at one sitting — converges on a single preconceived emotional effect, such as melancholy in 'The Raven' or escalating terror in 'The Fall of the House of Usher'; the ideal poem is short enough to preserve this total effect. (5) Transcendentalism: a New England philosophical and literary movement of the 1830s-50s within American Romanticism. Features: emphasis on spirit, or the Oversoul, as the most important thing in the universe, with nature as its symbol; belief in intuition over logic and the senses; self-reliance, the divinity of man and optimism about human perfectibility. Leading figures: Ralph Waldo Emerson (Nature, 'the Bible of New England Transcendentalism', and 'The American Scholar') and Henry David Thoreau (Walden) (高分笔记4, p14, p17).

questions.stem: Explain Imagism, the American Dream, the Lost Generation, Black Humor and Theatre of the Absurd.
questions.referenceAnswer: (1) Imagism: an early-20th-century literary movement led by Ezra Pound, characterized by the use of precise imagery and clear, economical language, breaking with Victorian rhetoric; Pound, 'the father of modern American poetry', was its leading figure, and his two-line 'In a Station of the Metro' is the famous example (高分笔记5, p32-33). (2) The American Dream: the national creed that everyone, through hard work and initiative, can achieve material success and upward advancement regardless of origin. American literature both celebrates and indicts it: Gatsby's romantic pursuit and Willy Loman's destruction dramatize its betrayal, turning the dream into a critical mirror of American society. (3) The Lost Generation: the post-WWI generation of American writers (Hemingway, Fitzgerald, etc.) who were disillusioned by the war and became expatriates. Their writings center on the war and its aftermath, are often autobiographical, and treat decadence and the death of the American Dream; Hemingway's The Sun Also Rises (1926) is the emblematic work (高分笔记5, p12-13, p15). (4) Black Humor: a literary device and postwar school in novels and plays that discusses taboo, gruesome or painful subjects while adding an element of comedy — 'a humor out of despair and laughter out of tears' — satirizing hypocrisy, racial prejudice and the dehumanization of the individual; Joseph Heller's Catch-22 (1961) is the representative work (高分笔记6, p5, p8). (5) Theatre of the Absurd: a dramatic genre originating in the mid-20th century among European and American dramatists of the 1950s and early 1960s, resting on the existentialist sense that, with transcendental roots lost, man is abandoned and all his actions become senseless, absurd and useless; it expresses this through non-realistic forms — illogical plots, repetitive dialogue and meaningless waiting — as in Beckett's Waiting for Godot and Edward Albee's plays (高分笔记3, p2; 高分笔记6, p27-28).

questions.stem: Define dramatic monologue and describe the Metaphysical Poets.
questions.referenceAnswer: (1) Dramatic monologue: a lyric poem in which a single fictional speaker addresses a silent audience at a dramatic moment or crisis. In listening to this one-sided talk — in which the speaker argues his case and unconsciously reveals his own character, motives and state of mind — the reader forms his or her own opinions and judgments about the speaker. It was the dominant poetic medium of Robert Browning ('My Last Duchess', in which the Duke's polished speech exposes his arrogance, possessiveness and cruelty) and was also mastered by Tennyson ('Ulysses') (高分笔记2, p67, p87-88). (2) The Metaphysical Poets: a loose group of 17th-century British lyric poets writing under the influence of John Donne, including George Herbert and Andrew Marvell. Samuel Johnson described them as a school of highly intellectual poetry marked by bold and ingenious conceits, incongruous imagery, complexity of thought, frequent paradox and deliberate harshness of expression. Their works tend to psychological analysis of the emotions of love and religion, draw images from actual life, and are characterized by simple diction, mysticism in content and fantasticality in form; the extended metaphor known as the 'metaphysical conceit' (e.g. Donne's comparison of parted lovers to a drawing compass) is their signature device (高分笔记1, p55-56).

questions.stem: Explain chivalric romance and the Shakespearean sonnet.
questions.referenceAnswer: (1) Chivalric romance: the popular medieval literary form — a long composition, sometimes in verse, sometimes in prose — used to sing the adventures, quests and courtly love of knights and other heroic deeds. Drawing on the Matter of Britain (the Arthurian legend: Sir Gawain, Launcelot, Merlin, the Holy Grail), it typically combines French and Saxon elements and dramatizes tests of faith, courage, purity and moral weakness; Sir Gawain and the Green Knight is the culmination of the Arthurian romances (高分笔记1, p16-17). It flourished in the Medieval English period (1066-1485) alongside the ballad, its popular counterpart (2019 年名词解释原题, 高分笔记1, p10). (2) The Shakespearean sonnet: the sonnet form Shakespeare used — a 14-line poem, usually in iambic pentameter, consisting of three quatrains rhyming abab cdcd efef and ending with a rhyming couplet gg. The theme is put forward and developed in the three quatrains, and the couplet ends the poem with a surprise conclusion or a shift of ideas. Shakespeare's sequence of 154 sonnets — divided into groups addressed to a young man and to the 'dark lady' — treats love, the destructive power of time and the immortality of verse (Sonnet 18: 'So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, / So long lives this, and this gives life to thee') (高分笔记1, p32; 2019 年名词解释原题, 高分笔记1, p25).

questions.stem: Discuss learner-related factors that influence second-language learning.
questions.referenceAnswer: Learner-related (internal) factors that influence second language learning include: (1) Motivation, the single most striking factor - instrumental vs integrative motivation, integratively motivated learners being more likely to succeed; later views add cognitive/resultative motivation, since achievement in turn sustains motivation. (2) Language aptitude, the special ability for learning a second language, a conglomerate of abilities: phonemic coding ability, grammatical sensitivity, inductive language-learning ability and rote-learning ability (Carroll and Sapon), with working memory central in newer models. (3) Age: children are better learners in pronunciation while adults are advantageous in cognitive capabilities; age does not change the route of acquisition. (4) Learning strategies: metacognitive strategies (e.g. selective attention), cognitive strategies (e.g. inferencing) and social/affective strategies (e.g. asking for clarification); successful learners use more and more varied strategies. Together with social factors such as language policy and social demand, these individual differences largely explain variation in L2 outcomes.

questions.stem: Define soliloquy and place Moll Flanders in English novel history.
questions.referenceAnswer: (1) Soliloquy: the act of talking to oneself, whether silently or aloud; in drama it denotes the convention by which a character, alone on the stage, utters his or her thoughts aloud. Playwrights use it as a convenient device to convey information about a character's motives and state of mind, for purposes of exposition, and to guide the judgments and responses of the audience. Marlowe's Dr. Faustus opens with a long expository soliloquy and concludes with another expressing Faustus' frantic attempts to escape damnation; the best-known of all dramatic soliloquies is Hamlet's 'To be, or not to be' (高分笔记1, p34; 2020 年名词解释原题, 高分笔记1, p25). (2) Moll Flanders in English novel history: Moll Flanders (1722) is Daniel Defoe's more mature piece after Robinson Crusoe, written in an autobiographical form called memoirs and narrated as the adventures of its female protagonist. Its historical significance is threefold: Defoe — the first writer to study lower-class people and regarded as the founder of the 18th-century English realistic novel — introduces for the first time a lowly woman as the subject of literature; the novel anticipates later works that take women as the center of attention in order to expose how the social system victimizes them; and it stands with Robinson Crusoe and Richardson's Pamela at the rise of the English novel in the 18th century, a fiction of ordinary life, morality and domestic manners (高分笔记2, p16, p27, p49; 2020 年名词解释原题, 高分笔记2, p3).

questions.stem: Define stream of consciousness and sentimentalism.
questions.referenceAnswer: (1) Stream of consciousness: a narrative mode that assumes a person's most significant existence lies in the mental and emotional world rather than the outside world; influenced by Freud's theory of the unconscious, it holds that mental life is not linear and logical but fragmentary and associative, and that the writer's task is to reveal this psychological reality in words. Woolf defines it as following the lines of a character's thoughts as they occur — describing unspoken thoughts without resorting to conventional dialogue. Masters: James Joyce (Ulysses), Virginia Woolf (Mrs Dalloway) and William Faulkner (The Sound and the Fury) (高分笔记3, p4, p13, p15; 高分笔记5, p25; 2021 年名词解释原题, 高分笔记3, p2). (2) Sentimentalism: an 18th-century English literary trend that arose as a reaction against neoclassical rationality and cold reason, indulging in emotion, sympathy and tears for the poor, the suffering and the wronged in order to awaken the reader's moral feeling; its reliance on subjective points of view made it a forerunner of the modern psychological novel. Representatives: Tobias Smollett, Laurence Sterne (Tristram Shandy; A Sentimental Journey — himself a forerunner of stream of consciousness) and Goldsmith (The Vicar of Wakefield) (高分笔记2, p9-10; 2021 年名词解释原题, 高分笔记2, p3).

questions.stem: Define ballad and critical realism.
questions.referenceAnswer: (1) Ballad: a narrative poem or song that tells a story in short stanzas. A ballad usually opens abruptly and gets to the point immediately, because its audience already knows the characters and plot; it concentrates on a single dramatic episode, narrates the story through dialogue and action, and is marked by theatricality; its theme is usually tragic. Subjects range from warfare, bloodshed and superstition to domesticity and exile; the 'border ballads' of the Anglo-Scottish frontier and the Robin Hood ballads celebrating the outlaw's fight against oppressors are the most famous (高分笔记1, p16-17). (2) Critical realism: the dominant mode of the Victorian novel (and of 19th-century European fiction generally), which gives a truthful depiction of people's lives while launching bitter and strong criticism of capitalist society — its money-worship and Utilitarianism, hypocrisy, poverty and injustice — so as to awaken the public consciousness to social problems and to promote reform. Victorian critical realists set their plots against a broad social background with strong cause-effect sequences and a pronounced moral purpose; Charles Dickens is its greatest representative, exposing in novel after novel the poverty, hypocrisy and corruptness around him, and the tradition runs through Thackeray, the Brontës, George Eliot to Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles (高分笔记2, p63-65, p68-69).
questions.analysis: ballad 是中世纪通俗叙事文类（2019 年同卷曾考 chivalric romance，两者恰成'雅俗对照'），答'突变式开头+单一事件+对话与动作+悲剧性'即可；critical realism 是维多利亚文学的核心概念，必须扣住笔记关键词 'Critical realism, Expose and Attack'——真实描写与揭露批判缺一不可。常见失分点：只答'现实主义'而丢掉 critical（批判性、唤醒公众意识）这一层；ballad 漏掉与 romance 的对比。

questions.stem: Define language acquisition, syntactic categories, referential meaning and conceptual metaphor theory.
questions.referenceAnswer:
Language acquisition: the natural process of children's language development, i.e. picking up the mother tongue subconsciously in social communication; by extension, second language acquisition is the process by which a language other than the mother tongue is learnt in a natural setting or in a classroom.
Syntactic categories: a syntactic category is a class of words or phrases that can substitute for one another without loss of grammaticality, e.g. NP, VP, PP, Det, Adj, Aux; in "A naughty boy broke the window", "a naughty boy", "he", "John" all belong to the category NP.
Referential meaning: the central and most stable part of word meaning - the relation by which a word picks out or identifies an entity in the world (e.g. dog denotes a kind of domestic animal), as opposed to the less stable, more culture-specific associative meanings (connotative, social, affective, reflected, collocative).
Conceptual metaphor theory: the cognitive-semantic view that metaphor is not a rhetorical decoration but a cognitive device essential to thought. We understand an abstract, less-structured target domain in terms of a concrete, familiar source domain through systematic correspondences called mapping, e.g. LIFE IS A JOURNEY (birth = beginning of journey, death = reaching destination). Metaphors are systematic, create similarities between domains, and unite reasoning and imagination.

questions.stem: Answer three prompts: how culture influences language; how communicative competence differs from linguistic competence; and how intake differs from input.
questions.referenceAnswer:
(1) How culture influences language: language is influenced and even shaped by culture; it is culturally loaded and culturally dependent, and culture exerts a strong influence particularly on the semantic structure of language and on its actual use in social communication (connotations and associations of culturally loaded words vary across cultures). Language is not only a system of symbols but also a socio-cultural activity, which accounts for the design feature of cultural transmission; without a cultural environment, language acquisition would be out of the question.
(2) Communicative competence vs linguistic competence: linguistic competence, in Chomsky's sense, is the tacit knowledge of the language system itself (its grammar). Communicative competence, proposed by Hymes and others, covers both the tacit knowledge of language and the ability to use it appropriately: the speaker can judge whether something is formally possible, feasible, appropriate and actually done. It thus adds rules of use - when to speak, to whom, in what manner - and underlies communicative syllabuses, which develop grammatical, sociolinguistic, discourse and strategic competence.
(3) Intake vs input: input is the target-language data the learner is exposed to, while intake is what is actually assimilated. Gass distinguishes the two and treats intake as a process which mediates between target language input and the learner's internalized set of rules: not all input is noticed, not all noticed input is comprehended, and not all comprehended input becomes intake. Output can in turn become new input through interaction.

questions.stem: Define derivation, language and linguistics, semantics and pragmatics, compounding, minimal pair, phoneme, free variation and assimilation rule.
questions.referenceAnswer:
Derivation: the word-formation process of adding a derivational affix to an existing base to construct a new word (happy -> unhappy, good -> goodness); it may change the grammatical category, the meaning, or both, and the words formed are called derivatives.
Language and linguistics: language is a system of arbitrary vocal symbols used for human communication; linguistics is the scientific study of language - linguistic phenomena are observed, hypotheses are formulated and tested, and linguistics studies language both as a system of sound, structure and meaning and in relation to society and mind.
Semantics and pragmatics: semantics is the study of meaning, the analysis of conventional meanings of words and sentences out of context ("what does X mean?"); pragmatics is the analysis of meaning in context, dealing with the relationships between linguistic forms and their users (speaker meaning, contextual meaning, inference of invisible meaning).
Compounding: the combination of two or more free morphemes into one word (bookshelf, greenhouse). The rightmost morpheme determines the word class, the leftmost takes primary stress, and the meaning is not always the sum of the components (a greenbottle is a kind of fly).
Minimal pair: two words that differ by only one sound in the same position and differ in meaning (zip/sip, pin/bin), showing that the two sounds are in contrastive distribution and are separate phonemes.
Phoneme: the smallest phonological unit in a language that can distinguish meaning; an abstract unit of the speaker's mental representation, written between slashes, and realized in context by allophones (/m/ and /b/ in mat/bat).
Free variation: sounds that appear in the same phonetic position and can substitute for each other without any change of meaning; they are often dialectal variants (e.g. economics with /i:/ or /e/).
Assimilation rule: a phonological rule by which a sound becomes more like a neighboring sound. Progressive assimilation: the preceding sound influences the following one (the devoicing rule, e.g. play, snow); regressive assimilation: the following sound affects the preceding one (the nasalization rule, e.g. bean, bomb).
questions.analysis: 八个定义的大集合，逐个"定义+要点/例子"：派生（笔记Chapter4 p.6）、复合（p.6：左重音右词性、词义非简单相加）、语言与语言学（Chapter1 pp.3、9：任意性声音符号系统；观察-假设-验证的科学）、语义学与语用学（Chapter6 p.2、Chapter7 p.18：脱离语境的规约义 vs 语境中的使用义）、最小对立体（Ch3 p.10）、音位（pp.9-10：能区别意义的最小音系单位、抽象心理表征）、自由变体（p.11：同位置可替换不改义）、同化规则（pp.11-12：顺同化/逆同化）。失分点：音位漏"抽象单位/由音位变体实现"；自由变体漏"替换不改变意义"。

questions.stem: Answer ten short questions: distinguish greenhouse/green house; explain creativity; define taboo/euphemism and their relation; name Halliday's language functions; name metaphor components; describe English stress/intonation functions; relate phonetics/phonology; contrast anaphoric/cataphoric reference with examples; assess componential analysis; distinguish homonyms/polysemes.
questions.referenceAnswer:
(1) Greenhouse vs green house: "a greenhouse" = an indefinite article + a compound noun; primary stress falls on green, and it means a glass building used for growing plants. "A green house" = an indefinite article + a modifier + a noun; stress falls on house, and it means a house whose color is green. Stress distinguishes both the structure and the meaning.
(2) Creativity/productivity: a design feature of human language - language provides opportunities for sending messages that have never been sent before and for understanding novel messages. The grammatical rules and words of a language are finite, but the sentences are infinite; even a child can put sounds and words into novel combinations. This feature is not found in animal communication systems.
(3) Taboo and euphemism: taboo is a prohibition on the use of, mention of, or association with particular words, objects, actions or persons (in English mostly body parts, bodily functions, distressing things and death). Euphemism is the avoidance of words which may be offensive or disturbing, substituting milder expressions (pass away for die). Relationship: taboos and euphemisms are two sides of the same coin - taboos are usually expressed through euphemisms; both are dependent on context and culture-specific, and euphemisms are in flux (crisis - depression - recession).
(4) Halliday's language functions: the three metafunctions - the ideational function (language as a symbolic code representing the world and our experience), the interpersonal function (language as a medium to get along in a community, to thank, apologize, argue, comfort) and the textual function (organizing messages into coherent texts that fit their co-text and context).
(5) Components of metaphor: the source domain (concrete and familiar), the target domain (usually abstract or less well structured), and mapping - the transference of properties from the source domain to the target domain by virtue of correspondences between the two (LIFE IS A JOURNEY).
(6) Functions of English stress and intonation: first, to highlight the information focus (the nucleus is stressed, the vowel lengthened, followed by a slight pause); second, to eliminate ambiguity - stress distinguishes compound from phrase (greenhouse vs green house) and intonation distinguishes sentence meanings and attitudes (falling for assertion and wh-questions, rising for yes/no questions).
(7) Phonetics and phonology: both study speech sounds but from different perspectives. Phonetics studies how speech sounds are produced, what phonetic features they have and how to transcribe them; phonology studies sound systems and patterns - which sounds distinguish meaning, how sounds vary in context, and which sequences are possible. Phonetics assumes invariant segments; phonology studies variation.
(8) Anaphoric vs cataphoric reference: anaphoric reference points backward to a preceding antecedent - "A boy and a girl are planting a tree. She is holding it and he is shoveling earth around it." Cataphoric reference points forward to a following expression - "When I saw her, Mary looked ill."
(9) Componential analysis: analyzing word sense by decomposing it into atomic semantic features (man: +HUMAN +ADULT +MALE). Merits: it made a breakthrough in the formal representation of meaning, revealed imprecise terminology, and handles hyponymy (father contains all the features of man). Limitation: it cannot be applied to the whole lexicon, only to words within the same semantic field.
(10) Homonyms vs polysemes: homonyms have the same form but different, unrelated meanings (bank: financial institution / side of a river); a polyseme is one word with several related senses (drink). Criteria for telling them apart: native speakers' intuition; etymology (same origin - polysemy; different origins - homonymy); dictionary treatment (polysemous senses under one heading, homonyms under different headings).
questions.analysis: 回忆型十小问，须逐条对应作答，跨Ch1/3/4/5/6/7/8。高频要点：greenhouse 复合词左重音、玻璃暖房 vs 绿房子（笔记Chapter3 p.15）；创造性（Ch1 pp.3-4）；禁忌语与委婉语一体两面、依赖语境与文化（Ch9 pp.14-15）；Halliday 三元功能（Ch1 p.7）；隐喻成分 source/target/mapping（Ch6 p.13）；重音语调两功能：突出信息焦点+消歧（Ch3 pp.14-15）；语音学与音系学视角之别（Ch3 p.9）；前指/后指方向与例句（Ch7 p.20）；成分分析优点与局限（Ch6 pp.8-9）；同形同音词与多义词三分判据：直觉、词源、词典（Ch6 p.7）。

questions.stem: Discuss features of modern linguistics; Searle's intentionality in pragmatics with examples; and Grice's implicature theory compared with Austin's speech-act work.
questions.referenceAnswer:
Modern linguistics has four features. First, priority is given to spoken language, because speech is historically prior to writing, serves a much wider range of communicative purposes, is structurally more complex, and is acquired earlier. Second, its focus is synchronic rather than diachronic: linguists are more interested in contemporary language than in the evolution of languages. Third, it is descriptive and explanatory rather than prescriptive: it states objectively how a language is spoken and explains why, instead of laying down rules. Fourth, it is theoretically rather than pedagogically oriented, striving to construct theories that account for language in general rather than reference books for teaching.

Searle develops Austin's speech act theory through the notion of intentionality. In pragmatics, meaning is intentional meaning: in uttering a sentence the speaker's mind is directed at the world through intentions, and what is communicated is the speaker's intended meaning or illocutionary force. The same sentence "It's cold in here" can be a statement, a request to close the window, or a complaint, depending on the speaker's intention and the context. Searle systematizes this insight: utterance acts succeed under felicity conditions, illocutionary acts fall into five classes (assertives, directives, commissives, expressives, declarations), and in indirect speech acts one illocutionary act (e.g. a request) is performed by way of another (e.g. a question, "Why don't you go with us?"), which the hearer recovers by inference.

Grice attacks meaning from the inferential side. His Cooperative Principle, with the maxims of quantity, quality, relevance and manner, assumes that conversational participants cooperate; when a speaker flouts a maxim, the hearer computes a conversational implicature - implicit meaning beyond what is said. Compared with Austin, Grice's theory is inferential rather than act-based: Austin asks what people DO in saying something (locutionary, illocutionary, perlocutionary acts), while Grice asks how MORE is communicated than is said. The two are complementary: speech act theory describes the acts performed by utterances, and implicature theory explains how their indirect force is worked out; together they show that meaning in use is intention-based, context-dependent and inferential.
questions.analysis: essay 三段：现代语言学四特征（笔记Chapter1 p.11：重口语、共时、描写解释、理论取向）；Searle 的意向性（Chapter7 pp.18、21-23：语用学研究意向的说话人意义；适切条件、五分类、间接言语行为；宜配 It's cold in here 一句多义例）；Grice 与 Austin 比较（pp.21-25：Austin 行为论——言内/言外/言后；Grice 推理论——合作原则与含义；二者互补而非对立）。失分点：三部分只各自罗列不做比较；Searle 部分不举例、意向性空泛。

questions.stem: British literature: define allegory, Neoclassicism and Metaphysical Poets; comment on Shakespeare's contribution; describe the historical/cultural background of the English Renaissance; discuss the rise of the English novel and Dickens as a critical realist.
questions.referenceAnswer:
(1) Allegory: a narrative in which characters, settings and events carry a second, systematic level of abstract — moral, religious or political — meaning. Spenser's The Faerie Queene is a long allegorical poem planned in 12 books (six finished): a complex moral, religious and political allegory exalting Queen Elizabeth I and the English nation, readable both as a romantic narrative of the Red Crosse Knight's chivalric adventures and as a spiritual allegory of the Christian's struggle for salvation (高分笔记1, p36; 2016 年名词解释原题, 高分笔记1, p25).
(2) Neoclassicism: the 18th-century English literary trend developed under the intellectual influence of the European Enlightenment. It modelled itself on Greek and Latin authors and tried to control literary creation by fixed laws and rules; reason was stressed, so writings were didactic and satirical, elegance, correctness, appropriateness and restraint were preferred, and the closed (heroic) couplet was regarded as the only possible verse form for serious work; its artistic ideals were order, logic and restrained emotions. Pope (An Essay on Criticism, its manifesto work) and Samuel Johnson are the leading representatives (高分笔记2, p8-9).
(3) Metaphysical Poets: a loose group of 17th-century British lyric poets under the influence of John Donne (Herbert, Marvell), described by Samuel Johnson as writing highly intellectual poetry marked by bold and ingenious conceits, incongruous imagery, complexity of thought, paradox and deliberate harshness of expression; their themes are love, death and religion, their diction simple, with mysticism in content and fantasticality in form (高分笔记1, p55-56).
(4) Shakespeare's contribution: he stands at the summit of the English Renaissance. His achievements: (a) one of the founders of realism in world literature — his histories register the decay of feudal nobility, his comedies paint life and love freed from feudal fetters, his great tragedies (Hamlet, Othello, King Lear, Macbeth) depict the life-and-death struggle of humanists against the dark forces; (b) he adapted plots freely from Greek legends, Roman history, Italian stories and English chronicles, fusing classical form with English content; (c) his plays voice the desires and aspirations of the English people, are permeated with patriotism, optimism and humanist praise of love, nature and human dignity, and expose social inequality and religious persecution; (d) he was skilled in every poetic form — song, sonnet, couplet and dramatic blank verse; (e) he was a great master of the English language, adding many words and phrases to everyday English (高分笔记1, p38-41).
(5) Historical/cultural background of the English Renaissance: economically, the Enclosure Movement and the flourishing clothing industry created the capitalist and laboring classes and stimulated commercial expansion abroad; politically, the war with Spain proclaimed the triumph of the rising bourgeoisie over declining feudalism, England established her first colonies, and the Elizabethan Age brought peace, prosperity and the Queen's own literary interest; culturally, the introduction of printing accelerated the spread of books and knowledge; intellectually, the society in transition from feudalism to capitalism produced the Renaissance and Humanism, which exalted human dignity, potential and present life rather than the afterlife (高分笔记1, p29-31).
(6) The rise of the English novel and Dickens as a critical realist: the 18th century saw the rise of the novel in Defoe (Robinson Crusoe, Moll Flanders — the founder of the English realistic novel and the first writer to study lower-class people) and Richardson (Pamela), with Fielding, 'the father of the English novel' (Tom Jones, Joseph Andrews), perfecting its comic-epic form; these fictions focused on morality and domestic manners, and Austen later brought the novel to maturity. In the Victorian age the novel flourished — thanks to a new reading public, dropping book prices, professional authorship and the need for entertainment and satire — and its dominant mode became critical realism: plots against a broad social background, strong cause-effect sequence, and a marked moral purpose exposing money-worship, poverty and injustice. Dickens is its supreme practitioner: he maps the whole 19th-century urban world (especially London), builds complicated constructions with minor or parallel plots, is a great humorist and satirist, and makes the novel 'the instrument of morality and justice', exposing all the poverty, hypocrisy and corruptness he saw around him (Oliver Twist, David Copperfield, A Tale of Two Cities) (高分笔记2, p16, p27, p49, p63-65, p68-69).

questions.stem: American literature: define Puritanism, American Naturalism and Black Humor; comment on Edgar Allan Poe; discuss stream of consciousness in Faulkner, American poetry of the Romantic period and twentieth-century American drama.
questions.referenceAnswer:
(1) Puritanism: the beliefs and practices of the English Protestants who sought to purify the Church of England and, escaping religious persecution, emigrated in the early 17th century to New England (Massachusetts Bay Colony, 1629) to build an ideal Christian commonwealth. Its literature is marked by religious devotion (salvation, piety, the God-man relation), moral and didactic content, self-examination in spiritual autobiographies recording conversion and the struggle with sin, and a plain, unornamented style; it shaped the American cultural identity of individualism and self-reliance, and its heritage of sin, guilt and redemption later pervades Hawthorne and Melville (高分笔记4, p2-4; 2020、2024 年名词解释原题, 高分笔记4, p2).
(2) American Naturalism: a movement of the late 19th to early 20th century, an advanced stage or extreme form of realism inspired by natural science, especially Darwinism. It holds that man's life is determined by heredity and environment; naturalists reflect reality in an extremely objective way, without moral judgement, and are more ironic. Representatives: Stephen Crane (The Red Badge of Courage), Jack London (The Call of the Wild), Theodore Dreiser (Sister Carrie) (高分笔记5, p1, p3-4; 2019、2023、2024 年名词解释原题).
(3) Black Humor: a literary device used in novels and plays to discuss taboo subjects while adding an element of comedy — a humorous way of treating serious, gruesome or painful things, 'a humor out of despair and laughter out of tears', satirizing hypocrisy, racial prejudice and the dehumanization of the individual by modern science; Joseph Heller's Catch-22 (1961) is the representative work (高分笔记6, p5, p8).
(4) Comment on Edgar Allan Poe: Poe was at once poet, short-story writer and critic. As a writer he explores the dark and mysterious side of the human psyche ('The Fall of the House of Usher') and the abyss of grief and loss: 'The Raven' turns the mourning for dead Lenore into a hypnotic poem of repetition in which the bird's 'Nevermore' defeats every hope of reunion, dramatizing the victory of the irrational over reason. As a critic he formulated the theory of the unity of effect — a short tale or poem, readable at one sitting, must be composed so that every element converges on a single preconceived emotional effect — laying the foundation of the modern short story and of American art-for-art's-sake aesthetics (高分笔记4, p11, p31-33; 2024 年简述原题, 高分笔记4, p10).
(5) Stream of consciousness in Faulkner: Faulkner, Nobel laureate of 1949, shares with Joyce and Woolf the primary narrative technique of stream of consciousness — a mode of narrative that follows the lines of a character's thoughts as they occur, letting readers enter the mind and become participants rather than observers, as in Benjy's time-less, fragmentary section of The Sound and the Fury. He combines it with the multiple point of view: different narrators (Benjy, Quentin, Jason and an omniscient voice) react differently to the same events, reflecting the psychological complexity of the characters and making the truth difficult to see; the technique serves his great theme of the decline of the Southern aristocracy (高分笔记5, p22-25).
(6) American poetry of the Romantic period: Walt Whitman — Leaves of Grass, a collection of more than 300 poems in free verse, in which grass, 'the most common thing with greatest vitality', images the rising American nation and his ideals of democracy, freedom and equality; he celebrates the individual, the common people and the body and soul of man. Emily Dickinson — her poems grow out of personal experience, treating religious doubt, love, and above all death and immortality, dense with image in every word (a forerunner of Imagism), as in 'I heard a Fly buzz — when I died'. Edgar Allan Poe — 'The Raven', a poem of beauty, death and musical repetition. These poets gave American literature its first independent, distinctly national voice (高分笔记4, p6, p10-11, p33, p41; 2024 年简述原题, 高分笔记4, p10).
(7) Twentieth-century American drama: Eugene O'Neill, the founder of American modern drama, brought serious tragedy to the American stage; his autobiographical Long Day's Journey into Night depicts one day of the Tyrone family — father, morphine-addicted mother and two sons — in a tragedy of fate and family. Arthur Miller wrote social and psychological drama: Death of a Salesman (1949), 'the tragedy of a man who gave his life, or sold it, in pursuit of the American Dream', makes the common salesman Willy Loman a tragic figure and critiques the dream that turns human beings into products. Edward Albee, leader of the American Theatre of the Absurd in the 1960s, dramatizes the meaninglessness of life and the difficulty of communication in The Zoo Story and Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? (高分笔记5, p39-40; 高分笔记6, p25-29).

questions.stem: 解释原型范畴理论中的 prototype。

questions.stem: Discuss practical applications of linguistics and insights about language/learning that inform teaching decisions; give an example.
questions.referenceAnswer:
语言描写为大纲、教材提供内容和术语；语言与习得研究帮助教师决定教什么、怎么教。例如功能语言学促使课程兼顾语法形式与交际功能。

展开（英文作答参考）：Linguistics contributes to foreign language teaching in two ways. (1) Applications: the products of linguistic description provide the input to syllabus design and material construction - without linguistic descriptions it is hard to define the content of a language course, and the metalanguage makes it possible to talk about what is to be taught. Descriptions of sounds, words, sentences, meaning and discourse therefore determine what appears in a structural or communicative syllabus and in textbooks. (2) Implications: the insights gained by linguists into the nature of language and the process of language learning help decision-makers and teachers decide what to teach and how to teach. At the preparatory level specialists draw on linguistics, psychology and pedagogy to design syllabuses; at the operation level the teacher's view of language shapes his teaching: a formal view highlights structures, a functional view adds functional items needed for communication, and a communicative view aims at developing learners' communicative competence. Example: informed by functional linguistics, a course may organize units around functions such as apologizing, thanking and requesting while still teaching the underlying grammar; informed by SLA research on input, intake and interaction, teachers add pair work and information-gap tasks so that output becomes new input. Linguistics is also indispensable to language testing and to the professional development of language teachers - it sharpens their awareness of the nature of language, the complexity of language learning, and the identification and diagnosis of learner errors.
questions.analysis: 考Chapter 12语言学与外语教学（笔记Chapter12 p.33）：applications——语言描写成果为大纲设计与教材编写提供输入、元语言使"谈教什么"成为可能；implications——语言观与习得研究帮助决策者与教师决定教什么、怎么教（准备层面与操作层面）。essay 需展开并举例（如功能语言学使大纲兼顾语法形式与交际功能项）。失分点：只答"语言学对教学有用"而不落到大纲/教材/教师语言观三个层面。

questions.stem: 概述 Geoffrey Chaucer 对英国文学的贡献。
questions.referenceAnswer: Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343-1400), whom Dryden calls 'the father of English literature', made four-fold contributions. (1) Language and verse form: writing in Middle English (the London dialect) instead of French or Latin, he helped establish English as the literary language of the country; he introduced from France the heroic couplet — rhymed iambic pentameter lines in pairs — and various rhymed stanzas, replacing the Old English alliterative verse (高分笔记1, p14, p16). (2) Narrative realism: his masterpiece The Canterbury Tales gives a comprehensive realistic picture of 14th-century feudal society; the pilgrims, drawn from almost every class (royalty and peasants excepted), combine typical qualities with individual dispositions, and the work covers all the major medieval genres — courtly romance, beast tale, folk tale, sermon and adventure story (高分笔记1, p14). (3) Humanism: taking the standpoint of the rising bourgeoisie, Chaucer affirms men and opposes the church dogma of asceticism, praising human energy, intellect and love of life, with gentle satire and mild irony — he is the forerunner of English Humanism (高分笔记1, p14). (4) Legacy: he pioneered English narrative poetry and set the model for the great English verse tradition that runs through Spenser, Shakespeare and beyond.
questions.analysis: 乔叟是中古英语时期的核心考点（笔记1 p3 复习指导明确提示其'文学贡献'为简答常考）。答题按四步走：语言贡献（英语文学语言化+英雄双韵体）→《坎特伯雷故事集》的现实主义群像与文类集大成→人文主义先驱→'英国文学之父'地位。常见失分点：漏掉 heroic couplet；把乔叟归入文艺复兴作家（他是中世纪向文艺复兴过渡的人物，笔记将其置于 Medieval Period）。

questions.stem: 评述英国文学中的唯美主义。
questions.referenceAnswer: Aestheticism was an intellectual and art movement of the latter part of the 19th century (the fin-de-siecle Victorian age) which insisted that aesthetic values, rather than social-political or moral themes, should dominate literature, fine art and music. It arose in opposition to the dominance of scientific thinking and to the indifference or hostility of middle-class society towards any art that was not useful or did not teach moral values. Its creed is summed up as 'art for art's sake': a work of art is the supreme value among human products precisely because it is self-sufficient, having no use or moral aim outside its own being — the end of a work of art is simply to exist in its formal perfection, to be beautiful and to be contemplated as an end in itself; art should be judged by beauty, not by morality or reason. In England the movement's theorist was Walter Pater and its chief representative Oscar Wilde — The Picture of Dorian Gray dramatizes the worship of beauty and sensory experience, and Wilde's preface and comedies ('There is only one thing in the world worse than being talked about, and that is not being talked about') turned aesthetic doctrine into social legend. Evaluation: Aestheticism liberated art from Victorian utilitarianism and moralism and paved the way for modern aesthetics and Symbolism, but its cult of beauty and indulgence in excess also exposed the danger of art cut off from life (高分笔记2, p68; 2015 年名词解释 'art for art's sake' 原题, 高分笔记2, p61).
questions.analysis: 唯美主义=维多利亚晚期流派，'评述'题须两面兼顾：先答定义（为艺术而艺术、艺术自足、反对功利与道德说教）与王尔德《道连·格雷的画像》，再作评价（解放了艺术观念，但形式至上导致与生活脱节）。常见失分点：只答'为艺术而艺术'一句而不展开'艺术自足性'的内涵；与自然主义（左拉，同属 19 世纪后期但立场相反）混淆；漏掉王尔德这一代表人物。

questions.stem: 简述英国第一代浪漫主义诗人。
questions.referenceAnswer: English Romanticism is usually dated from 1798, when Wordsworth and Coleridge published the Lyrical Ballads — the collection whose preface defines poetry as 'the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings' and is regarded as the manifesto of the movement (高分笔记2, p28, p31, p35). The first-generation poets are the elder, 'escapist' romanticists — Wordsworth, Coleridge and Southey, known as the Lake Poets because they lived in the Lake District: frightened by the coming of industrialism and the nightmare towns, they turned to nature for protection and reflected the nostalgia of old rural England. William Wordsworth: the leading figure, who worshipped nature as the revelation of truth and drew poetry from ordinary rustic life and plain language ('I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud'; 'The Solitary Reaper'), defining poetry as emotion recollected and overflow. Samuel Taylor Coleridge: the poet of imagination and the supernatural, whose The Rime of the Ancient Mariner and Kubla Khan treat mysterious, exotic subjects with dreamlike imagery, supplying Romanticism's theory of imagination. General features these poets established: expressiveness in place of the neoclassical mirror, creative imagination, love of the strange and supernatural, and the worship of nature (高分笔记2, p34-35).
questions.analysis: 第一代浪漫主义诗人=湖畔派三诗人（Wordsworth、Coleridge、Southey），起点必须落在 1798 年《抒情歌谣集》与'强烈情感的自然流露'。关键区分：第一代是 'escapist romanticists'，因恐惧工业化而退向自然寻求庇护；第二代（Byron、Shelley、Keats）是 'active romanticists'，积极表达变革理想——这条两代对照线是评分要点（笔记2 p35 原文）。常见失分点：把 Blake、Burns（前浪漫主义）或 Scott 混入第一代；漏掉《抒情歌谣集》这一标志性合著。

questions.stem: 说明清教主义对美国文学的影响。
questions.referenceAnswer: Puritanism denotes the doctrines and practices of the English Protestants who sought to purify the Church of England and, escaping religious persecution, emigrated to New England in the early 17th century (Massachusetts Bay Colony from 1629) to reestablish an ideal place and restore the lost paradise. Its influence on American literature runs through form, theme and spirit. (1) Religious devotion: early American literature centers on salvation, personal piety and the relationship between God and humanity — sermons, religious tracts and devotional poems (高分笔记4, p2). (2) Moral and didactic content: Puritan writing teaches moral lessons, meant to instruct, warn and guide readers in a righteous life (高分笔记4, p3). (3) Self-examination: the spiritual autobiography recording one's conversion and struggle with sin becomes a native form, carried from Puritan diaries down to Franklin's Autobiography (高分笔记4, p3-4). (4) Plain style: plain, direct, unornamented language became a lasting feature of the American literary manner (高分笔记4, p3). (5) Cultural identity: Puritanism instilled individualism and self-reliance, values integral to the American ethos, and its sense of mission underlies American idealism (高分笔记4, p4). (6) Later literary heritage: its doctrines of original sin, guilt and redemption permeate the American Renaissance — Hawthorne's The Scarlet Letter and 'Young Goodman Brown' expose sin beneath the surface of Puritan goodness and criticize Puritan hypocrisy, while Melville probes good and evil in Moby-Dick (高分笔记4, p11, p18, p21-22; 2020、2024 年名词解释, 2025 年 15 分简答原题, 高分笔记4, p2).
questions.analysis: 这是 2025 年 15 分大题（笔记4 p2 真题表：Give a comment on the significance of Puritanism in American literature）。答题结构：一句定义+文学特征四点（宗教主题、道德说教、自省、平实文风）+文化精神影响（个人主义、自立）+后世作家例证（Hawthorne、Melville、Franklin）。常见失分点：只答清教定义不落到'文学影响'；漏掉 plain style 与自省传统；举例时只报名字不点出《红字》的罪与救赎主题。

questions.stem: 概述美国南方文学的历史背景、常见主题及代表作家。
questions.referenceAnswer: Southern literature grows out of the distinctive history of the American South: plantation slavery, defeat in the Civil War of the 1860s, Reconstruction, and the postwar decline of the old aristocratic families — a legacy of defeat, guilt, lost pride and decay that haunts the region's writing. (1) Historical background: the South's economy and social order rested on slavery and the plantation system; the Civil War abolished slavery and ruined the old wealth, yet the old families clung to outdated codes of chivalry and honor long after their material basis was gone (高分笔记5, p22, p24). (2) Common themes: the burden of a historical past and memory; the decline and collapse of aristocratic families and of the ideal of the Southern lady and gentleman; race and class conflict; the clash between traditional agrarian values and modern industrialization; sin, guilt and the struggle for endurance. (3) The Southern Renaissance: the cultural and literary movement that rejuvenated Southern literature in the 1920s and 1930s, facing the region's contradictions with realistic seriousness (高分笔记5, p8, p21). (4) Representative writers: William Faulkner is the most important figure — awarded the 1949 Nobel Prize, he set 19 novels and numerous stories in his fictional Yoknapatawpha County (Jefferson, modeled on his hometown Oxford, Mississippi): The Sound and the Fury chronicles the physical, mental and moral decline of the Compsons; 'A Rose for Emily' renders the pride and decay of a Southern gentlewoman. Eudora Welty ('Death of a Traveling Salesman') is another representative of the region (高分笔记5, p9, p21-27; 2025 年 15 分简答原题, 高分笔记5, p9).
questions.analysis: 南方文学是 2025 年 15 分大题（笔记5 p9 真题表：Elaborate on the Southern Literature in the US），题干三问对应'背景—主题—代表作家'三段式作答。背景扣奴隶制、内战战败与旧南方贵族衰落；主题扣历史包袱、家族没落、种族与阶级冲突；作家以 Faulkner 为核心（约克纳帕塔法世系、《喧哗与骚动》《献给爱米丽的玫瑰》），可补 Welty。常见失分点：把南方文学答成泛泛的地域文学，漏掉 Southern Renaissance（南方文艺复兴）与内战历史创伤这两个关键词。

questions.stem: 简要介绍 Jane Austen。
questions.referenceAnswer: Jane Austen (1775-1817) is an English novelist who stands between the 18th and early 19th centuries: neither a Classicist nor a Romantic, she is best thought of as a pioneering figure in the development of the novel, providing the bridge between the two traditions and preparing the way for 19th-century realism (高分笔记2, p49). (1) Works: six novels — Sense and Sensibility, Pride and Prejudice (generally considered her most successful and popular work), Mansfield Park, Emma, Persuasion and Northanger Abbey (高分笔记2, p49). (2) Themes: courtship and marriage among the country gentry, and through them money, manners, morality and the situation of women, whose fate in her world depends almost entirely on marriage and property; her irony gently exposes snobbery, vanity and self-deception (e.g. Mr. Collins, Lady Catherine in Pride and Prejudice). (3) Art: delicate irony and satire; precise observation of 'the universal pattern of human behavior' within the small world of '3 or 4 families in a country village'; measured prose and controlled free indirect discourse presenting characters' inner deliberations — a technical step toward the modern psychological novel. (4) Significance: her sensitivity to universal patterns of human behavior brought the English novel to its maturity and won her an important place in the history of English literature (高分笔记2, p48-49).
questions.analysis: 奥斯丁答题四步：作品（六部小说，以《傲慢与偏见》为核心）→主题（婚姻、金钱与女性处境）→手法（讽刺、自由间接引语、日常生活的精细描写）→小说史地位（兼具古典与浪漫之间、把英国小说推向成熟、下启现实主义）。常见失分点：因与浪漫主义诗人同时代而把她归入 Romanticism（笔记2 p49 明确说她 'neither a Classicist nor a Romantic'，是过渡与桥梁人物）；只复述《傲慢与偏见》情节而不谈艺术手法。

questions.stem: 评述维多利亚时期的英国小说。
questions.referenceAnswer: The Victorian novel flourished against a sharply contradictory background. (1) Historical background: the Victorian Age (1837-1901) witnessed drastic economic expansion — Britain, the leading industrialized country, won the fame of 'the workshop of the world' — but industrialization made the struggle between capital and labour the central conflict after 1830; the ruling class preached 'Victorian virtues' (domesticity, self-reliance, self-help, probity) while the keyword of Victorian literature is anxiety (高分笔记2, p63). (2) Reasons for the flourishing of the novel: a new reading public, the dropping price of books, writing as a profession, the need for recreation and entertainment, the need for satire of individuals or institutions, and the feminist movement; serialization and periodical publication shaped the form (高分笔记2, p64). (3) Common features of Victorian novels: plots unfolded against a broader social background than before, reflecting the complexity of human relations in capitalist society; a much stronger cause-effect sequence; taint of the Puritan spirit of the age (strict sexual code, women as 'angels in the house'); and a marked moral purpose — writers wrote to edify readers and bring about reforms (高分笔记2, p64-65). (4) Critical realism: the dominant mode — a truthful depiction of people's lives combined with bitter and strong criticism of money-worship, Utilitarianism, and the widespread misery, poverty and injustice of capitalist society, awakening the public consciousness to its social problems (高分笔记2, p63-64). (5) Representatives: Charles Dickens, the greatest critical realist, who maps the whole 19th-century urban world and makes the novel the instrument of morality and justice (Oliver Twist, David Copperfield, A Tale of Two Cities); W. M. Thackeray (Vanity Fair); the Brontë sisters; George Eliot; and Thomas Hardy, who carried the tradition to its end with Tess of the d'Urbervilles (高分笔记2, p61, p67, p68-69).
questions.analysis: 评述题按'背景—小说繁盛原因—共同特征—批判现实主义—代表作家'五段展开；其中'维多利亚小说共同特征'四点（社会背景更广阔、因果情节更强、清教气息、道德目的）是笔记原文考点（笔记2 p64-65），必须逐点写出。常见失分点：只罗列作家名单而不分析特征；漏掉'繁盛原因'（新读者群、书价下降、职业写作、连载）这一采分点；把维多利亚小说与 18 世纪小说的兴起混为一谈。

questions.stem: 简评 Henry David Thoreau。
questions.referenceAnswer: Henry David Thoreau (1817-1862), American essayist, poet and practical philosopher, was a leading New England Transcendentalist renowned for having lived — not merely preached — its doctrines. (1) Life and thought: a man full of dreams and ideals, he wrote about nature and the philosophy of life; he spoke out on peace, living simply and the abolition of slavery, and was a vigorous advocate of civil liberties and individual conscience against unjust social institutions (高分笔记4, p17-18). (2) Walden (1854): his masterwork, a collection of 18 essays recording the two years (1845-47) he lived in a cabin he built himself by Walden Pond near Concord, Massachusetts. A believer in the Transcendentalist idea of self-reliance, he builds his own house and grows his own food in his bean-field, preferring solitude and believing in the power of work, individuality and living according to one's ideals; the book is principally a record of his thoughts and observations and is celebrated as a foundational work of American nature writing (高分笔记4, p17-18). (3) Critique of civilization: he hated human injustice and the slavery system, criticized modern civilization for having dehumanized man, attacked society's pretensions and excesses, and urged men to simplify their lives and escape societal institutions in order to elevate their lives (高分笔记4, p18). (4) Significance: together with Emerson's Nature — 'the Bible of New England Transcendentalism' — Walden turned Transcendentalist theory into a way of life; Thoreau's example of non-conformity and civil disobedience has since inspired environmental thought and movements of peaceful resistance (高分笔记4, p14, p17-18).
questions.analysis: Thoreau 是 2026 年 15 分真题（笔记4 p10 真题表：Gave a briefly comment on Henry David Thoreau）。答题扣三条线：超验主义实践者（与爱默生《论自然》对读：《瓦尔登湖》是理论的'生活化'）→《瓦尔登湖》关键词（self-reliance、solitude、simplicity、nature）→社会批判面（废奴、公民不服从、对物质文明的反思）。常见失分点：只讲'湖边隐居'的故事而不上升到哲学与社会批判；漏掉 self-reliance 这一超验主义核心词。

questions.stem: 介绍犹太裔美国文学的主要主题和代表作家。
questions.referenceAnswer: Jewish American literature refers to the rich and diverse body of writing produced by Jewish authors in the United States, primarily throughout the 20th and 21st centuries; it is deeply tied to the mass migration of Jews to America (chiefly from Eastern Europe) around the turn of the 20th century, and encompasses drama, fiction and poetry (高分笔记6, p29-30). (1) Major themes: identity and assimilation — balancing assimilation into America with the preservation of Jewish cultural and religious tradition; intergenerational conflict between immigrant parents and their American-born children; Jewish identity in the American context; the memory of persecution and of historical events such as the Holocaust; the immigrant's economic and social upward struggle, treated with humor and irony (高分笔记6, p30). (2) Representative writers: Saul Bellow, Nobel Prize-winning author known for his intellectual and philosophical novels (e.g. Herzog, Henderson the Rain King); Bernard Malamud, whose fiction (e.g. The Assistant) blends Jewish suffering with redemptive compassion; Philip Roth (e.g. Portnoy's Complaint), who probes Jewish family, self-invention and the anxieties of assimilation. Earlier figures such as Abraham Cahan opened the immigrant tradition (高分笔记6, p30). (3) Significance: from the immigrant margins, Jewish American writers moved to the very center of postwar American fiction, giving universal artistic expression to the predicament of the modern outsider and of minority identity in America.
questions.analysis: 犹太裔美国文学在笔记6 有专节（p29-30 考点九），是 2026 年新考点的直接来源。答题三段：移民史背景（东欧犹太移民大潮）→主题（同化与身份平衡、代际冲突、大屠杀记忆、双重文化处境）→代表作家（Bellow 诺奖、Malamud、Roth，逐人一句定位）。常见失分点：与 Harlem Renaissance 等其他族裔文学混淆；只报作家名单而写不出'同化 vs 文化保存'这一主题核心。

questions.stem: 评述第二代英国浪漫主义诗人。
questions.referenceAnswer: The second generation of English Romantic poets — Byron, Shelley and Keats — are the younger, 'active' romanticists: unlike the Lake Poets, who turned to nature for protection, they expressed the aspirations of those oppressed by capitalism and held out the ideal of a future society free from oppression and exploitation (高分笔记2, p35). (1) George Gordon Byron: creator of the 'Byronic hero' — the proud, passionate, rebellious outcast of Childe Harold's Pilgrimage and the oriental tales — and the great satirist of European society in Don Juan; his restless revolt against tyranny culminated in his death in the Greek War of Independence, making him the very image of the romantic rebel. (2) Percy Bysshe Shelley: the revolutionary idealist whose poetry prophesies change and rebirth — 'Ode to the West Wind' ('If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?', 2022 年转述原题, 高分笔记2, p31) makes the west wind the destroyer and preserver that scatters the seeds of a new world; Prometheus Unbound celebrates the overthrow of tyranny; his 'A Defence of Poetry' claims poets as 'the unacknowledged legislators of the world'. (3) John Keats: the poet of sensory beauty and of art's power to defeat time. His great odes — 'Ode to a Nightingale' and 'Ode on a Grecian Urn' ('Beauty is truth, truth beauty') — set mortal anguish against immortal art; he also formulated the doctrine of negative capability, the ideal of open-mindedness, of 'letting the mind be a thoroughfare for all thoughts' (2023 年评论原题, 高分笔记2, p31; 高分笔记2, p48). Though all three died young, their poetry carried English Romanticism to its climax, and Coleridge-to-Scott dating marks the movement's end at Scott's death in 1832 (高分笔记2, p35).
questions.analysis: 第二代浪漫主义诗人=Byron、Shelley、Keats（active romanticists，笔记2 p35）。三人各有一个标签作答：拜伦——Byronic hero 与讽刺（Don Juan）；雪莱——政治理想与变革预言（《西风颂》）；济慈——感官美与艺术的永恒（希腊古瓮颂）+ negative capability。关键区分：第一代 escapist 退向自然，第二代 active 面向现实与革命。常见失分点：三代人归属混淆；negative capability 照字面直译而不作解释；漏掉《抒情歌谣集》之外的 1798-1832 年代框架。
